assigned.ownerDirectionVerbatim: I feel like they are still a little confusing and we may be missing some of the concepts that are most tested and testable. ... look up everything they can about that topic and decide what concepts on that are the most testable. Then look at all the questions that fit in that topic category and critically analyze if it is a good question based on the rules and feedback you have gotten from me on what is a good and what is a bad question. Then the worker also looks for gaps on that topic that it can fill in with more questions. Remember to try to create multiple part questions when possible. ... The goal of this is to increase the number of questions, fill gaps, test the testable stuff, and to make the current existing questions better and more accurate. Also remember that the questions need to be difficult.

priorIndependentReview.title: Intermittent pediatric groin swelling

cues.phrase: The bulge returns into the abdomen with gentle pressure. The abdomen is soft, the groin is not tender, and he has continued eating and passing stool.
cues.why: The cluster of reassuring observations makes Arrange emergency groin exploration readily dismissible even without detailed pediatric surgical knowledge. These are necessary urgency findings to retain, but they leave a weak emergency competitor.

cues.phrase: bowel sounds are heard over the bulge today
cues.why: Alongside the loop-shaped moving structure, this strongly announces enteric rather than fluid-only contents. It is a raw clinical observation, not literally a diagnosis label, but substantially pre-resolves the hydrocele-versus-hernia distinction for a resident.

fairness: Node node.n4.intermittent-groin-contents-versus-fluid-scan.v1: planned inguinal herniotomy is the defensible best offered plan for the current reducible enteric groin findings without the described signs of an acute complication. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in that ranking.

The quiet fluid-only scan does not create a necessary second inference: deleting the entire previous-ultrasound sentence leaves the same straightforward diagnosis and disposition. The task remains familiar reducible-hernia recognition followed by routine elective-versus-emergency triage.

The options compare three plans, but continued hydrocele follow-up is contradicted by the current findings and emergency exploration is contradicted by reducibility and the reassuring course. Neither offers a close residual decision for a PGY-2/3 resident. twoStep is false under the owner's consequential-reasoning standard, despite the nominal diagnose-then-treat sequence.

The parent video describes an externally visible loop-shaped movement, not verified anatomical contents. It should not be treated as direct visualization of bowel through the skin. The current clinical examination already carries the decision, so this uncertain interpretation is unnecessary to defend the key; no confident claim of physical impossibility is made.

Clinic phase, named child and caregiver fit. No treatment deadline or age cutoff is inferred. The unspecified duration of a hypothetical hydrocele would also prevent this item from teaching a general observation policy for hydroceles at this age.
suggestions: Retain reducibility, tenderness and obstructive-symptom information. Seek explicit acceptance as basic recognition/triage, or develop a verified residual decision that these findings do not already settle.
Make any prior imaging discrepancy necessary to the revised choice; otherwise remove it rather than counting historical conflict as an additional reasoning step.

Describe a parent video as observable swelling behavior without claiming it establishes tissue identity. Use credible current plans rather than a fluid-only diagnosis and an unsupported emergency operation as the main distractors.

rankedConcepts.decision: Reassess the urgency of evolving neonatal intestinal obstruction.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Changing urgency can prevent ischemic bowel delay.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Recognize a completed positive rotational study and an acquired decline despite resuscitation.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Repeat contrast because that was the correct earlier pathway.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Clinician must check the operative-versus-imaging ranking; no resection extent or exact resuscitation target is taught.

rankedConcepts.decision: Assess an incomplete contrast study in neonatal bilious vomiting.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Study adequacy is distinct from a negative result.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret the acquisition record as a gastric/duodenal-bulb examination, not an assessment of the entire duodenal course.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Accept gastric emptying as exclusion of malrotation and obtain a pyloric study.
rankedConcepts.consequence: BAPM supports the contrast pathway; the acquisition-adequacy inference is an original application. No radiographic image interpretation is claimed.

rankedConcepts.decision: Use residual chloride and acid-base disturbance when judging operative readiness.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Normal potassium does not establish complete resuscitation.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret the discordant recovery: circulation and potassium improved, but chloride-depletion alkalosis persists.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Proceed after urine output and potassium normalize.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Exact readiness thresholds and fluid composition require current local pediatric/anesthesia review; no fixed delay is prescribed.

rankedConcepts.decision: Select management after partial ileocolic reduction with persistent stability.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Partial progress and adverse predictors require an actual tradeoff.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret partial anatomical progress and trapped fluid separately: residual disease remains, but a risk predictor does not itself prohibit another enema.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Operate immediately because trapped fluid and incomplete reduction are overread as absolute failure.
rankedConcepts.consequence: The repeat attempt is reasonable, not compulsory. A clinician must confirm the local radiology/surgery decision and quality of the closest operative alternative.

rankedConcepts.decision: Escalate persistent intussusception after failed repeat reduction and a structural lead point.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Treatment failure plus a structural lesion changes the next action.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret repeated nonprogress and a moving intraluminal lesion as persistent structural disease, not uncomplicated recurrence.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Choose another enema because recurrence can often be treated nonoperatively.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Specific operative extent and pathology are intentionally not predicted. No exact universal number of enema attempts is taught; the two sessions are fictional course data.

rankedConcepts.decision: Resolve inadequate rectal histology before diagnosing Hirschsprung disease.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Specimen adequacy controls justification for definitive surgery.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Identify that the report describes absent sampling of the relevant tissue, not a represented submucosal plexus without ganglion cells.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Proceed from the phrase no ganglion cells as if it established disease, or repeat only the contrast study.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary definitive surgery or continued misclassification could follow.

rankedConcepts.decision: Choose structural assessment after pull-through despite ganglionated tissue.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Innervation and mechanical patency are different evidence.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret the current biopsy as evidence of innervation, not proof that the anastomosis and pull-through are mechanically unobstructed.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Order manometry because the normal ganglion cells are overread as excluding any surgical cause.
rankedConcepts.consequence: A correctable structural problem could be missed or a functional treatment given prematurely.

rankedConcepts.decision: Interpret a fixed bowel loop against improving NEC physiology.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: A traditional imaging sign must be reconciled with response.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Distinguish persistent loop position from documented perforation or proven bowel necrosis.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Laparotomy because fixed loop has been memorized as an absolute trigger.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary intervention could follow, while treating an isolated sign as reassuring in every context would also be unsafe.

rankedConcepts.decision: Escalate NEC after failure of a bridging peritoneal drain.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: A patent device is not proof of controlled disease.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret a patent drain and low free-fluid burden as evidence against simple device failure, not as proof of viable bowel.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Replace a functioning drain rather than investigate the uncontrolled bowel problem.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Definitive bowel assessment could be delayed.

rankedConcepts.decision: Choose closure strategy after physiologic intolerance of complete reduction.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Anatomy and reversible physiologic response change closure technique.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Identify the reversible coupled ventilatory and perfusion response to complete reduction.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Select sutureless closure to avoid tension while repeating the same intolerable full reduction.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Respiratory or splanchnic/peripheral perfusion compromise could recur.

rankedConcepts.decision: Apply cardiopulmonary status to giant omphalocele closure strategy.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Defect type and pulmonary status alter closure strategy.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret intact sac, external liver and limited domain as a giant omphalocele context rather than exposed-bowel gastroschisis.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Choose staged reduction because a large defect cannot be closed primarily.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Reduction could worsen an already compromised cardiopulmonary state.

rankedConcepts.decision: Select nonoperative decompression for uncomplicated meconium ileus.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Patency, intraluminal material and resuscitation alter decompression.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret contrast reaching the ileum and outlining pellets as evidence of a luminal meconium problem rather than a discontinuous atretic segment.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Immediate surgery because small colon has been memorized as synonymous with atresia.
rankedConcepts.consequence: An unnecessary operation or an unsafe enema before adequate resuscitation could follow.

rankedConcepts.decision: Apply the COG framework to a typical unilateral resectable childhood renal mass.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: A tissue-first exception depends on protocol and resectability.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Assess the unilateral renal origin and intact-resection anatomy as a typical resectable Wilms context.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Biopsy every suspected malignant mass before definitive treatment.
rankedConcepts.consequence: A biopsy can upstage otherwise resectable COG disease and change subsequent therapy.

rankedConcepts.decision: Plan regional nodal staging despite normal-appearing nodes.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Reassuring gross observations cannot replace microscopic staging.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret imaging and inspection as insufficient evidence about microscopic nodal involvement.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Omit nodes because both CT and inspection are reassuring.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Understaging can alter adjuvant treatment selection.

rankedConcepts.decision: Use major-vessel involvement to choose tissue strategy for an extrarenal pediatric mass.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Origin and vascular risk defeat a generalized no-biopsy rule.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpret extrarenal location and urinary metabolites as a neuroblastic pattern while recognizing that tissue characterization is still needed.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Complete resection because the mass is localized, or nephrectomy by analogy with Wilms.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Major vascular injury or unnecessary nephrectomy could result.

rankedConcepts.decision: Balance prematurity-related respiratory risk against reducible hernia risk.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: Real respiratory/incarceration tradeoff replaces generic referral.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Recognize a reducible hernia without current incarceration while interpreting ongoing prematurity-related respiratory disease.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Require before-discharge repair solely because this is a child, despite current respiratory comorbidity.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary respiratory morbidity or, at the opposite extreme, an unmonitored delay could follow.

rankedConcepts.decision: Select a repeat study after inadequate assessment of suspected pyloric obstruction.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value resident application by editorial judgment; no exam-frequency claim.
rankedConcepts.priorityReason: A technically unsuccessful scan is not an adequate negative.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Infer a gastric-outlet pattern from feed-related nonbilious vomiting and weight loss.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Choose upper-GI contrast after misclassifying the outside ultrasound as a true negative.
rankedConcepts.consequence: The supporting local guideline is overdue for review; no unsupported ultrasound cutoff or diagnostic accuracy is used.

priorReview.title: Intermittent pediatric groin swelling

cues.phrase: The bulge returns into the abdomen with gentle pressure. The abdomen is soft, the groin is not tender, and he has continued eating and passing stool.
cues.why: The cluster of reassuring observations makes Arrange emergency groin exploration readily dismissible even without detailed pediatric surgical knowledge. These are necessary urgency findings to retain, but they leave a weak emergency competitor.

cues.phrase: bowel sounds are heard over the bulge today
cues.why: Alongside the loop-shaped moving structure, this strongly announces enteric rather than fluid-only contents. It is a raw clinical observation, not literally a diagnosis label, but substantially pre-resolves the hydrocele-versus-hernia distinction for a resident.

fairness: Node node.n4.intermittent-groin-contents-versus-fluid-scan.v1: planned inguinal herniotomy is the defensible best offered plan for the current reducible enteric groin findings without the described signs of an acute complication. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in that ranking.

The quiet fluid-only scan does not create a necessary second inference: deleting the entire previous-ultrasound sentence leaves the same straightforward diagnosis and disposition. The task remains familiar reducible-hernia recognition followed by routine elective-versus-emergency triage.

The options compare three plans, but continued hydrocele follow-up is contradicted by the current findings and emergency exploration is contradicted by reducibility and the reassuring course. Neither offers a close residual decision for a PGY-2/3 resident. twoStep is false under the owner's consequential-reasoning standard, despite the nominal diagnose-then-treat sequence.

The parent video describes an externally visible loop-shaped movement, not verified anatomical contents. It should not be treated as direct visualization of bowel through the skin. The current clinical examination already carries the decision, so this uncertain interpretation is unnecessary to defend the key; no confident claim of physical impossibility is made.

Clinic phase, named child and caregiver fit. No treatment deadline or age cutoff is inferred. The unspecified duration of a hypothetical hydrocele would also prevent this item from teaching a general observation policy for hydroceles at this age.
suggestions: Retain reducibility, tenderness and obstructive-symptom information. Seek explicit acceptance as basic recognition/triage, or develop a verified residual decision that these findings do not already settle.
Make any prior imaging discrepancy necessary to the revised choice; otherwise remove it rather than counting historical conflict as an additional reasoning step.

Describe a parent video as observable swelling behavior without claiming it establishes tissue identity. Use credible current plans rather than a fluid-only diagnosis and an unsupported emergency operation as the main distractors.

nodes.currentUpdate: Liam Carter's outside pediatric surgical record confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis by ultrasound. He remains on gastric decompression after initial IV resuscitation; nonbilious gastric losses continue.
nodes.task: Which perioperative plan is most appropriate for Liam Carter now?

items.label: Response to resuscitation
items.value: Peripheral perfusion and urine output have recovered.

items.label: Current laboratory results
items.value: Sodium 138 mmol/L; potassium 4.1 mmol/L; chloride 83 mmol/L; bicarbonate 39 mmol/L; venous pH 7.55.

choices.label: Continue IV correction before pyloromyotomy
choices.rationale: The chloride and acid-base values show substantial unresolved chloride-depletion alkalosis despite the improved circulation and potassium. Continue directed IV correction and replacement of losses before anesthesia.
choices.temptation: Recognize that initial circulatory improvement is not the full preoperative endpoint.
choices.correctUnder: Clinically meaningful chloride-depletion alkalosis remains after initial resuscitation.

choices.label: Begin pyloromyotomy during IV correction
choices.rationale: Definitive repair is needed, but beginning now treats recovered perfusion and normal potassium as sufficient while substantial alkalosis remains. This is not an arbitrary rule that any reference-range deviation forbids anesthesia.
choices.temptation: Prioritize definitive relief once circulation and potassium improve.
choices.correctUnder: Hydration and the clinically important electrolyte and acid-base disturbances have also been corrected.

choices.label: Continue IV maintenance before pyloromyotomy

nodes.objective: Apply the hepatic-vein-level caval-extension exception to initial treatment of presumed Wilms tumor under a COG pathway.
nodes.currentUpdate: Noah Bennett's outside pediatric oncology center uses the COG/North American Wilms pathway. The team is selecting his initial treatment sequence for a renal mass.
nodes.task: Which initial tumor-directed sequence should the outside team select for Noah Bennett?

items.label: Anatomic imaging
items.value: A mass expands the right renal parenchyma. The left kidney is normal. Enhancing tissue extends continuously from the right renal vein into the vena cava; its upper edge reaches the hepatic-vein confluence.

items.label: Specialist review
items.value: The imaging appearance is typical of Wilms tumor. The staging review shows no distant lesions.

choices.label: Biopsy, preoperative chemotherapy, then resection
choices.rationale: The caval extension reaches the hepatic veins, an exception to the usual up-front nephrectomy pathway. Under the stated framework, obtain histology and use preoperative chemotherapy before reassessing resection. The usual caution about biopsy upstaging does not erase this exception.
choices.temptation: Apply the vascular extent and the named protocol together.
choices.correctUnder: Presumed Wilms tumor whose caval extension reaches the hepatic-vein level.

choices.label: Nephrectomy with thrombectomy, then chemotherapy
choices.rationale: Up-front nephrectomy is usual for a typical resectable unilateral mass, but the superior caval extent changes the preferred sequence here. Localized staging does not by itself establish that immediate thrombectomy is the right first step.
choices.temptation: Generalize the usual COG surgery-first pathway to every unilateral tumor without metastatic disease.
choices.correctUnder: A typical unilateral tumor without the high caval extension or another preoperative-treatment exception can undergo up-front resection.

choices.label: Preoperative chemotherapy, then resection histology
choices.rationale: This sequence postpones the tissue diagnosis until resection. The named COG pathway for this exception calls for biopsy with preoperative therapy; a different treatment framework should not be silently substituted.
choices.temptation: Use a familiar preoperative-chemotherapy paradigm without retaining the stated COG histology requirement.
choices.correctUnder: A protocol explicitly permitting initial treatment of a typical renal mass without pretreatment biopsy governs the patient.

nodes.explanation: The caval extension reaches the hepatic veins, an exception to the usual up-front nephrectomy pathway. Under the stated framework, obtain histology and use preoperative chemotherapy before reassessing resection. The usual caution about biopsy upstaging does not erase this exception.

reasoning.interpretation: Recognize continuous renal-vein and caval extension and locate its superior extent at the hepatic veins rather than merely label a unilateral renal tumor.
reasoning.decision: Apply the COG vascular exception and preserve its pretreatment histology requirement when selecting the sequence.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Perform up-front nephrectomy and thrombectomy because the tumor is unilateral and staging is localized.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The upper end of continuous enhancing intravascular tissue reaches the hepatic-vein confluence.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Major high-caval surgery could be undertaken before the recommended preoperative-treatment assessment, or therapy begun under an unstated protocol.
reasoning.deletionTest: Removing the upper caval extent makes usual COG surgery-first plausible. Removing the named COG framework makes chemotherapy before resection histology a competing paradigm. Contralateral normality avoids a separate bilateral exception.
reasoning.counterfactual: If imaging instead confined the venous extension to the renal vein below the cava, with otherwise suitable unilateral resection anatomy and no other preoperative-treatment exception, nephrectomy with thrombectomy followed by chemotherapy becomes the best offered sequence.

authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Recognize continuous renal-vein and caval extension and locate its superior extent at the hepatic veins rather than merely label a unilateral renal tumor. nodes.objective: Interpret the tissue actually submitted before declaring regional Wilms staging complete.
nodes.currentUpdate: Noah Bennett is undergoing outside nephrectomy for presumed unilateral Wilms tumor under a COG/North American pathway. Before closure, the surgeon reviews the regional sampling record.
nodes.task: Which regional-node plan should the outside team select before completing Noah Bennett's operation?

items.label: Nodal assessment
items.value: Preoperative imaging shows no suspicious regional nodes. The visible hilar and periaortic nodes are small and soft.

items.label: Submitted specimen
items.value: The only separate specimen was labelled right hilar tissue. The pathologist reports the entire submitted fragment as mature adipose tissue and small vessels, with no malignant cells identified.

choices.label: Submit hilar and periaortic node samples
choices.rationale: The reported fragment is fat and vessels, not a histologically assessed lymph-node sample. No malignant cells in that fragment cannot establish regional node status. Obtain actual regional samples rather than rely on normal appearance or perform formal clearance.
choices.temptation: Interpret specimen provenance before accepting a reassuring negative phrase.
choices.correctUnder: The intended nodal submission contains no represented lymph-node tissue.

choices.label: Close without further regional-node sampling
choices.rationale: The negative phrase applies to the tissue actually submitted. It does not establish that regional nodes were sampled, and their normal appearance is not a reliable substitute for histology.
choices.temptation: Read no malignant cells as a completed negative regional stage without checking specimen composition.
choices.correctUnder: The operative and pathology records already establish representative hilar and periaortic node sampling with no remaining suspicious basin or other staging concern.

choices.label: Perform formal retroperitoneal node clearance
choices.rationale: The unresolved task is staging with regional samples. Formal retroperitoneal clearance is not the required sampling operation and is not justified merely because the submitted fragment missed nodal tissue.
choices.temptation: Overcorrect an incomplete sample by treating sampling as a formal clearance indication.
choices.correctUnder: A separate, established oncologic indication for that operation exists; the current specimen error by itself is not such an indication.

nodes.explanation: The reported fragment is fat and vessels, not a histologically assessed lymph-node sample. No malignant cells in that fragment cannot establish regional node status. Obtain actual regional samples rather than rely on normal appearance or perform formal clearance.

reasoning.interpretation: The reassuring pathology result applies to fat and vessels, so it has not established the status of the intended lymph nodes.
reasoning.decision: Choose regional staging samples of the appropriate scope rather than omit further sampling or escalate to formal clearance.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Close because no malignant cells were found and both imaging and gross nodes appear reassuring.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The entire only submitted regional fragment contains adipose tissue and vessels; actual nodal tissue has not been represented.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: An unstaged regional basin may be incorrectly recorded as negative and affect subsequent treatment assessment.
reasoning.deletionTest: Removing specimen composition collapses the new tissue-provenance decision into the original sampling-rule recall. Removing normal gross findings weakens the credible temptation to accept the submitted negative phrase. The before-closure stage makes this a current completion decision, not an invented reoperation rule.
reasoning.counterfactual: If the report instead documented represented hilar and periaortic lymph nodes with negative histology, all suspicious basins had been sampled and no other staging issue remained, closure without further regional sampling becomes the best offered plan.

authorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: Restated tumor and COG context. Used the raw tissue description rather than a conclusion that nodal sampling failed. No decorative measurements or fixed node quota is supplied.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: All options are the regional operative completion plan before closure in the same operation.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: The reassuring pathology result applies to fat and vessels, so it has not established the status of the intended lymph nodes. Then Choose regional staging samples of the appropriate scope rather than omit further sampling or escalate to formal clearance.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate: a superficially benign pathology phrase is tempting only if its specimen provenance is ignored. Formal clearance remains the credible overtreatment error.
authorGate.oneBestAnswer: The entire only submitted regional fragment contains adipose tissue and vessels; actual nodal tissue has not been represented. Counterfactual: If the report instead documented represented hilar and periaortic lymph nodes with negative histology, all suspicious basins had been sampled and no other staging issue remained, closure without further regional sampling becomes the best offered plan.
authorGate.sequenceAndFiniteProfileAttack: Standalone named 5-year-old male outside-hospital record review. No prior answer, later episode or feedback is displayed; one finite profile preserves the constrained age and sex.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Re-solved with actual nodes represented in both named basins; closure then wins. The scenario supplies an intraoperative pathology communication without teaching routine frozen sections or a mandatory minimum count.
authorGate.remainingRisk: NCI supports actual regional nodal sampling and its scope. The constructed report is a provenance application; Melissa must confirm clinical realism and that additional samples are the best exact before-closure action.
authorGate.verdict: Revised once for independent review; author self-check is not PASS

nodes.objective: Balance prematurity-related respiratory risk against reducible hernia risk.
nodes.currentUpdate: Henry Parker was born at 26 weeks and remains in an outside neonatal unit. Discharge is being planned with ongoing respiratory follow-up.
nodes.task: Which repair-timing plan is most appropriate for Henry Parker's current groin finding?

items.label: Groin course
items.value: Pediatric surgical examinations repeatedly show an inguinal bulge that reduces completely. There have been no painful irreducible episodes, vomiting or skin changes.

items.label: Respiratory and follow-up context
items.value: He still needs oxygen for bronchopulmonary dysplasia. His family can attend surgical follow-up and has been taught the warning signs requiring urgent reassessment.

choices.label: Plan repair after the neonatal hospitalization
choices.rationale: For a currently reducible hernia in a very preterm infant with ongoing respiratory disease, a delayed planned repair with follow-up is reasonable. The timing balances respiratory risk against incarceration during the wait; it is not indefinite observation or a universal age rule.
choices.temptation: Apply the respiratory-risk and hernia-urgency findings together.
choices.correctUnder: Selected reducible hernia with substantial prematurity-related respiratory risk and a reliable follow-up plan.

choices.label: Plan repair before neonatal discharge
choices.rationale: Earlier repair limits the time exposed to incarceration risk, but carries respiratory tradeoffs in this infant. No current incarceration complication requires overriding the respiratory consideration in the offered comparison.
choices.temptation: Treat every pediatric hernia as requiring repair before the current hospitalization ends.
choices.correctUnder: A changed hernia course or patient/follow-up factors making delay less appropriate after specialist review.

choices.label: Use serial surveillance for spontaneous resolution
choices.rationale: The current record repeatedly demonstrates a hernia, rather than documented resolution. Its reducibility supports a planned timing discussion, not a presumption that repair will become unnecessary. Reassessment remains part of the delayed surgical plan.
choices.temptation: Treat the possibility of spontaneous resolution as sufficient reason to abandon a planned repair pathway.
choices.correctUnder: A subsequently resolved finding confirmed on surgical reassessment with a revised diagnosis/plan, not the repeatedly demonstrated current hernia.

nodes.explanation: For a currently reducible hernia in a very preterm infant with ongoing respiratory disease, a delayed planned repair with follow-up is reasonable. The timing balances respiratory risk against incarceration during the wait; it is not indefinite observation or a universal age rule.

reasoning.interpretation: Recognize a reducible hernia without current incarceration while interpreting ongoing prematurity-related respiratory disease.
reasoning.decision: Balance the competing hazards and choose a scheduled delayed strategy instead of a compulsory pre-discharge repair or indefinite surveillance.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Require before-discharge repair solely because this is a child, despite current respiratory comorbidity.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The hernia remains reducible without acute episodes while respiratory disease persists and follow-up is workable.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Unnecessary respiratory morbidity or, at the opposite extreme, an unmonitored delay could follow.
reasoning.deletionTest: Deleting respiratory disease removes the reason to favor delay; deleting the reducibility/episode history removes the safety boundary. Follow-up context is necessary to the real tradeoff rather than a permission that surgery is available.
reasoning.counterfactual: If painful irreducible episodes emerged or reliable follow-up could not be maintained, an earlier repair plan could become preferable after urgent specialist reassessment.

authorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: No exact repair age, trial threshold, oxygen dose or effect size is supplied. The two planned timing options are genuine competitors. The surveillance label names a positive strategy rather than advertising an incomplete plan; the persistent examination finding must be applied.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Timing of an already indicated pediatric repair; no technique or anesthesia comparison is smuggled in.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Recognize a reducible hernia without current incarceration while interpreting ongoing prematurity-related respiratory disease. Then Balance the competing hazards and choose a scheduled delayed strategy instead of a compulsory pre-discharge repair or indefinite surveillance.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: competing real harms distinguish this from the former obvious referral question. The clinical ranking is conditional and must be reviewed by Melissa.
authorGate.oneBestAnswer: The hernia remains reducible without acute episodes while respiratory disease persists and follow-up is workable. Counterfactual: If painful irreducible episodes emerged or reliable follow-up could not be maintained, an earlier repair plan could become preferable after urgent specialist reassessment.
authorGate.sequenceAndFiniteProfileAttack: Single node. No parent video or previous fluid-only scan supplies tissue identity; the actual pediatric surgical examinations establish the finding.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the superficial referral/urgency contrast with a respiratory-versus-incarceration tradeoff and removed the trial-specific age cutoff; re-solved all timing plans. Final option recheck removed the phrase without a repair plan from the surveillance label, kept the same documented-persistence discriminator and re-solved the three strategies. Exact clinical ranking still needs named review.
authorGate.remainingRisk: The 2025 syntheses differ on incarceration estimates. No disputed claim of zero incarceration risk is taught. Delayed timing is a reasonable patient-specific proposal, not universally mandatory.
authorGate.verdict: Draft for independent review; author self-check is not PASS

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: {patientName}'s outside pediatric surgical record confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis by ultrasound. He remains on gastric decompression after initial IV resuscitation; nonbilious gastric losses continue.
decisionNodes.stem: Which perioperative plan is most appropriate for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Continue IV correction before pyloromyotomy
answerChoices.rationale: The chloride and acid-base values show substantial unresolved chloride-depletion alkalosis despite the improved circulation and potassium. Continue directed IV correction and replacement of losses before anesthesia.

answerChoices.label: Begin pyloromyotomy during IV correction
answerChoices.rationale: Definitive repair is needed, but beginning now treats recovered perfusion and normal potassium as sufficient while substantial alkalosis remains. This is not an arbitrary rule that any reference-range deviation forbids anesthesia.

answerChoices.label: Continue IV maintenance before pyloromyotomy
answerChoices.rationale: Waiting on maintenance fluid without actively correcting the remaining deficit and replacing continuing gastric losses does not address the reason to defer repair. No particular fluid prescription or dose is being scored.

answerChoices.label: Attempt a delayed repeat image-guided enema
answerChoices.rationale: Substantial partial progress with ongoing stability supports considering a delayed repeat enema. Trapped fluid may lower success but does not independently prohibit nonoperative reduction.

answerChoices.rationale: Immediate operation becomes more compelling with deterioration, perforation or persistent failure without a reasonable repeat opportunity; this first attempt made progress while she remains stable.

answerChoices.rationale: Documented residual ileocolic intussusception with continuing cramps needs an active reduction plan rather than assuming the transient small-bowel pattern.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: {patientName}'s outside records describe constipation since early infancy, distension and poor weight gain. The pediatric team is reviewing her rectal biopsy before selecting the next investigation.
decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnostic step should the outside team select next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Obtain expert histology with calretinin studies
answerChoices.rationale: Representative tissue is already present. An initial H&E report without identified ganglion cells requires further expert histologic evaluation, including ancillary methods, before it is treated as confirmation of aganglionosis.

answerChoices.label: Obtain a new rectal biopsy specimen
answerChoices.rationale: A new sample would address a tissue-acquisition problem, but the current specimen already contains submucosa at a relevant site. Initial H&E nonvisualization does not by itself establish that new sampling is the next step.

answerChoices.label: Obtain anorectal manometry with reflex testing
answerChoices.rationale: Physiology may contribute to evaluation, but it does not settle the interpretation of the representative biopsy already obtained. Finish the histologic assessment rather than substitute a reflex result for it.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: {patientName} had a pull-through for biopsy-confirmed Hirschsprung disease eight months before this outside visit. She initially passed spontaneous stools; during the last two months, soft stools have become progressively difficult to evacuate and distension has returned.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation plan should the outside team select next for {patientName}'s recurrent postoperative obstruction?

answerChoices.label: Rectal examination plus contrast enema
answerChoices.rationale: Ganglionated tissue establishes innervation at the sampled sites; it does not show that the reconstructed bowel is patent or untwisted. Examine the rectum and define the postoperative anatomy before assigning the symptoms to a functional mechanism.

answerChoices.label: Rectal examination plus anorectal manometry
answerChoices.rationale: Outlet dysfunction is plausible, but normal ganglionation does not exclude a stricture, cuff problem or twist. The missing current anatomical assessment makes contrast evaluation the better next plan here.

answerChoices.label: Rectal examination plus colonic transit study
answerChoices.rationale: A transit study addresses movement through the colon. It does not establish the postoperative configuration that remains in question in this record. It can become relevant to a residual motility question after outlet and structural evaluation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which abdominal-wall plan should the outside team begin now for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Protect the sac and defer reduction during stabilization
answerChoices.rationale: For the current pulmonary compromise, ERNICA favors initial nonoperative care with delayed closure. This preference concerns avoiding an additional reduction burden now; it also applies when the alternative is gradual staged reduction, not just forceful primary closure.

answerChoices.label: Begin staged reduction now and close after reduction
answerChoices.rationale: Gradual reduction is a legitimate strategy for a giant omphalocele. The closest decision here is whether to start it during worsening respiratory support; current expert guidance favors nonoperative stabilization in this pulmonary subgroup. Staging is not inherently forceful or never appropriate.

answerChoices.label: Begin complete reduction now and close the fascia
answerChoices.rationale: Limited abdominal domain and the current respiratory course make complete reduction with primary closure a poor initial strategy. Primary closure remains appropriate for selected smaller defects in a suitable physiological state.

answerChoices.label: Repeat image-guided therapeutic contrast decompression
answerChoices.rationale: There is persistent obstruction, but the first therapeutic attempt produced anatomical and clinical progress. In this resuscitated infant without an operative complication, another supervised contrast attempt is preferred to declaring failure or assuming resolution. No universal attempt count or interval is implied.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: {patientName}'s outside pediatric oncology center uses the COG/North American Wilms pathway. The team is selecting his initial treatment sequence for a renal mass.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial tumor-directed sequence should the outside team select for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Biopsy, preoperative chemotherapy, then resection
answerChoices.rationale: The caval extension reaches the hepatic veins, an exception to the usual up-front nephrectomy pathway. Under the stated framework, obtain histology and use preoperative chemotherapy before reassessing resection. The usual caution about biopsy upstaging does not erase this exception.

answerChoices.label: Nephrectomy with thrombectomy, then chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Up-front nephrectomy is usual for a typical resectable unilateral mass, but the superior caval extent changes the preferred sequence here. Localized staging does not by itself establish that immediate thrombectomy is the right first step.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative chemotherapy, then resection histology
answerChoices.rationale: This sequence postpones the tissue diagnosis until resection. The named COG pathway for this exception calls for biopsy with preoperative therapy; a different treatment framework should not be silently substituted.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: {patientName} is undergoing outside nephrectomy for presumed unilateral Wilms tumor under a COG/North American pathway. Before closure, the surgeon reviews the regional sampling record.
decisionNodes.stem: Which regional-node plan should the outside team select before completing {patientName}'s operation?

answerChoices.label: Submit hilar and periaortic node samples
answerChoices.rationale: The reported fragment is fat and vessels, not a histologically assessed lymph-node sample. No malignant cells in that fragment cannot establish regional node status. Obtain actual regional samples rather than rely on normal appearance or perform formal clearance.

answerChoices.label: Close without further regional-node sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The negative phrase applies to the tissue actually submitted. It does not establish that regional nodes were sampled, and their normal appearance is not a reliable substitute for histology.

answerChoices.label: Perform formal retroperitoneal node clearance

answerChoices.label: Plan repair after the neonatal hospitalization
answerChoices.rationale: For a currently reducible hernia in a very preterm infant with ongoing respiratory disease, a delayed planned repair with follow-up is reasonable. answerChoices.label: Plan repair before neonatal discharge

reviews.title: Bilious vomiting after an incomplete contrast acquisition
clarityIssues: The task 'Which investigation should follow Maya Wilson's current records?' is awkward: records are reviewed, while an investigation follows the clinical assessment. Ask for the next investigation for her ongoing bilious vomiting.
A soft abdomen does not by itself establish circulatory stability. The diagnostic pathway would be clearer with a concise current perfusion assessment.

cues.phrase: the remainder of the duodenal course was not imaged / Complete an upper-GI contrast examination
cues.why: An explicitly unfinished contrast examination pairs with the only option beginning 'Complete.' A reader can select completion rather than reason about what the acquired study excludes. The acquisition limitation is necessary information; the option-level completion cue is avoidable.

fairness: An upper-GI examination is the best offered investigation for ongoing neonatal bilious vomiting with an unassessed duodenal course. A reassuring plain film does not resolve the concern. No confident clinical error identified in that explanation.

Pyloric ultrasound is a weak competitor in this 3-day-old with dark-green emesis. The same answer follows after deleting the entire acquisition record, so that record does not supply a second consequential decision against these options.
This first node is self-contained. Its explanation identifies the unresolved rotational question but does not disclose the later operative answer.

Review scope: all 17 new executable nodes were assessed from their visible candidate fields, including prior explanations in paired cases. Three proposed-retirement historical records and the parked/held records were noted, not scored. This is an offline editorial review, not source verification or clinical approval; all drafts remain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: Use parallel investigation labels without making 'Complete' unique to the key.
Make acquisition adequacy change the decision between credible diagnostic paths; do not add more descriptions of the same missing examination. Preserve bilious emesis and necessary safety findings.
State current perfusion and use a direct next-investigation task. Retain the high-yield bilious-vomiting objective.

reviews.title: Volvulus with deteriorating perfusion

cues.phrase: the radiologist reports midgut volvulus
cues.why: The report supplies the diagnosis; the requested action is its familiar emergency treatment. A named diagnosis is permissible for management, but it removes the claimed interpretive step here.

cues.phrase: Perfusion and urine output worsen, and lactate rises despite IV fluid treatment / Proceed to urgent operative exploration
cues.why: Escalating danger pairs with the only urgent active treatment. The other options repeat a completed diagnostic study or continue already-failing support, making generic escalation sufficient.

fairness: Urgent exploration is clearly the best offered plan; the clinical explanation is sound. Resuscitation remains concurrent care, not an alternative to correcting volvulus.
Confirmed midgut volvulus already warrants urgent surgical treatment. The deterioration exhibit strengthens urgency but does not change the answer against these distractors.

The transition from incomplete to completed imaging is coherent, and this node states the decisive result independently. The preceding explanation does not explicitly supply surgery, although the pair predictably progresses from diagnosis to treatment.
suggestions: Retain the emergency findings. Either seek explicit acceptance as an easy safety-recognition item or test a distinct consequential operative decision using adequate findings and credible alternatives.
Do not manufacture difficulty by making repeat imaging or observation appear appropriate for documented volvulus. Removing the diagnosis label alone will not create two consequential steps.

reviews.title: Progressive nonbilious vomiting after limited ultrasound
clarityIssues: The explanation specifies 'expert targeted ultrasound,' but the answer label only specifies a repeat study. The case does not describe a changed acquisition approach that addresses the original gas limitation.

cues.phrase: The report lists the study as nondiagnostic / Repeat targeted pyloric ultrasonography
cues.why: An explicit failed-test conclusion and the same named anatomic target make repetition the obvious repair. The raw acquisition observations already establish the limitation; the interpretive label adds scaffolding.

fairness: Repeat expert ultrasound is a reasonable preferred approach, but upper-GI contrast is also a clinically credible investigation after an inconclusive ultrasound in persistent nonbilious vomiting. It is not reserved for bilious vomiting. The candidate needs a clearer basis for ranking those paths; I am not asserting that the proposed key is clinically wrong.
Contrast enema does not meaningfully compete for a gastric-outlet presentation. The item is mostly recognition of the usual first test plus a named adequacy problem.
This first node stands alone. Its explanation does not teach the subsequent metabolic-readiness answer.
suggestions: Have clinical review settle the repeat-ultrasound versus contrast-study boundary for this exact acquisition failure and describe any decision-critical technical difference neutrally.
Keep the acquisition observations, remove the redundant 'nondiagnostic' teaching label if it adds no information, and replace the lower-tract foil with a credible competing investigation or strategy.
Explain why the closest contrast-study alternative is less appropriate here without implying it has no role in evaluating nonbilious obstruction.

reviews.title: Pyloromyotomy timing after partial resuscitation
clarityIssues: Attempted milk feeds after ultrasound-confirmed obstruction and during preoperative correction are an awkward clinical sequence. The text does not say whether the feeding failure preceded confirmation.

cues.phrase: Vomiting recurs with attempted milk feeds / Defer pyloromyotomy for an oral rehydration trial
cues.why: The exhibit directly defeats the oral route, leaving a two-option contest. That distractor is particularly weak after established mechanical outlet obstruction.

fairness: The intended inference is meaningful: restored perfusion and normal potassium do not establish correction of the remaining chloride-depletion alkalosis. Further IV correction is the best offered plan on the intended reading.

Reference-relative laboratory descriptions can be sufficient and do not require invented thresholds. Nevertheless, 'outside the reference range' should not be taught as a universal anesthesia cutoff; the explanation should remain tied to unresolved clinically meaningful alkalosis. No exact readiness criterion was independently verified in this offline review.
The later node independently states the diagnosis and treatment response, and the preceding ultrasound explanation does not give away the timing decision.
suggestions: Clarify the feeding chronology or remove the milk-feed sentence and the oral-rehydration foil together.
Preserve the tension between clinical improvement and biochemical recovery, but compare credible perioperative plans instead of an oral trial for known obstruction.
Have Melissa confirm that the supplied laboratory description establishes a meaningful unresolved abnormality; use supported criteria if greater precision is necessary, not newly invented cutoffs.

reviews.title: Repeat reduction after substantial partial progress
fairness: The child has residual ileocolic disease, meaningful movement during the first enema, and preserved perfusion without guarding or perforation. Those observations support a repeat attempt over either assuming resolution or immediately treating the first partial reduction as definitive failure.

Two consequential judgments remain: distinguish incomplete but productive reduction from failure without progress, then apply the current safety findings despite the adverse fluid finding. Trapped fluid is clinically relevant evidence, not a nonmedical wording shortcut.

Older age deserves lead-point awareness but does not by itself make repeat enema wrong. No lead point is supplied in this first episode; the later mass must not be used retrospectively to answer this node.

The node stands alone. Its explanation supports considering repeat reduction rather than promising success or imposing a fabricated number of attempts. This is editorial PASS only, not clinical approval.
suggestions: Optional copyedit: change 'a 8-year-old girl' to 'an 8-year-old girl.' Preserve the clinically meaningful progress and safety observations.
Keep the later recurrent episode and its structural finding out of this node's pre-answer display.

reviews.title: Recurrent intussusception with failed reduction and a mass

cues.phrase: Two separate image-guided sessions produced no movement / Attempt another delayed image-guided enema
cues.why: The option repeats an explicitly ineffective intervention. Coupled with persistent symptoms, this supports a generic 'do something different' shortcut.

cues.phrase: a discrete intraluminal mass that moves with the leading edge / Perform operative reduction and assess the lead point
cues.why: Only the key offers to address the newly introduced structural finding and contains a second action. The other plans do not engage that finding.

fairness: Operation with assessment of the structural lesion is the best offered answer. The explanation appropriately grounds the decision in persistent failure and anatomy rather than age or recurrence alone.

Failure without progress and an apparent lead point both point to the same intervention; against these options they do not create two independent consequential steps. Passive observation is not a credible competitor for this symptomatic persistent ileocolic obstruction.

Chronology is coherent: full reduction occurred between episodes, and the current failure is explicitly described. The node stands alone, but the preceding explanation has already emphasized that partial progress supports another enema; reversing that taught feature makes this follow-up easier.
suggestions: Test a distinct clinically consequential decision after failed reduction, with plausible competing plans and the findings needed to distinguish them, or explicitly seek an accepted easy reinforcement role.
Avoid making the key uniquely comprehensive. Do not weaken or conceal genuine failed-reduction findings just to make further enemas appear attractive.
Copyedit 'a 8-year-old girl' to 'an 8-year-old girl.'

reviews.title: Inadequate rectal tissue in suspected Hirschsprung disease

cues.phrase: no submucosa / Repeat rectal biopsy with adequate submucosa
cues.why: The key literally supplies the named missing tissue. A reader does not need to know where ganglion cells are assessed to choose the option that repairs the explicitly stated omission.

cues.phrase: establish Ava Morgan's diagnosis before definitive surgery
cues.why: The definitive-diagnosis wording strongly favors histology over contrast imaging or physiology. A resident can select biopsy without interpreting this particular specimen.

fairness: The specimen cannot establish aganglionosis simply because no ganglion cells were found in tissue lacking submucosa. Representative rectal histology is the best offered confirmatory test; the nondiagnostic enema does not exclude disease.
The explanation is appropriately limited and does not equate the superficial result with a negative adequate biopsy. The problem is the bypassable reasoning, not a confident clinical inaccuracy.
The initial node stands alone. Its explanation does not disclose the later postoperative mechanical-assessment answer.
suggestions: Remove 'with adequate submucosa' from the pre-answer label and keep the tissue requirement in feedback; retain the actual specimen composition in the exhibit.

Use a neutral next-investigation task and a specimen-status decision that genuinely changes which investigation is justified, rather than asking the standard confirmatory test irrespective of the specimen.
Have clinical review specify the appropriate repeat sampling approach for this older child if procedure selection is intended; do not invent a depth or age threshold.

reviews.title: Persistent obstruction after a ganglionated pull-through
clarityIssues: The interval from pull-through and the postoperative bowel-function trajectory are unspecified. 'Persistent' could describe immediate recovery or an established later obstructive problem; this matters to the workup.

cues.phrase: she cannot tolerate further examination / anesthetized anorectal examination
cues.why: The key directly fixes the sole named unfinished procedure. It also bundles imaging with an examination while the other options each offer a single diagnostic modality.

cues.phrase: a recent representative biopsy ... contain normal ganglion cells / Repeat rectal biopsy with expert histopathology
cues.why: The distractor repeats a recent explicitly representative test with no supplied specimen or interpretive discrepancy. This makes it a disposable completed-test foil.

fairness: Structural assessment before assigning a functional outlet mechanism is a defensible preferred approach. Normal ganglionated tissue does not establish an anatomically unobstructed pull-through.

The intended two steps are worthwhile: interpret what the pathology excludes and what it does not, then sequence structural versus functional evaluation. The current option construction makes that sequence too easy to bypass.

The node independently states Hirschsprung disease, surgery and biopsy findings, so it does not require the preceding answer. The earlier histology explanation provides background but does not explicitly teach this key. Exact postoperative timing still needs clarification; I have not independently verified a mandatory test sequence.
suggestions: State whether bowel function never recovered or initially improved and then worsened, with a clinically supported postoperative context.
Compare similarly scoped diagnostic plans and remove the repeat-biopsy foil unless there is a genuine residual histologic uncertainty.

Keep the intolerance of awake examination if needed for procedure choice, but make interpretation of the postoperative findings, rather than matching 'cannot tolerate' to 'anesthetized,' determine the key.

reviews.title: Persistent radiographic loop during clinical improvement in NEC
fairness: The important conflict is visible: a persistent dilated loop versus improving abdominal findings, declining support and falling lactate, without reported free gas. Continued close nonoperative treatment is the best offered plan; the explanation does not claim the loop is harmless.

The learner must interpret the concerning radiographic persistence in context, then decide whether it outweighs the clinical response sufficiently to justify intervention. The improvement observations are decision-critical evidence, not a lexical cue to the answer.

Laparotomy is the meaningful competing error. Drainage is weaker without demonstrated perforation or instability but remains in the same intervention category. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

This first node stands alone and exposes no subsequent perforation. Its explanation does not preannounce the later rescue-laparotomy answer. Editorial PASS does not verify the cited guideline or confer clinical approval.
suggestions: Preserve the discordance between imaging and clinical course. Keep close reassessment explicit in feedback and do not convert this into an absolute rule against surgery whenever free gas is absent.

reviews.title: Clinical decline despite a functioning drain in perforated NEC
clarityIssues: The time course after drainage is not specified. The direction of deterioration is clear, but the response interval would help distinguish immediate peri-transfer instability from continued failure of the drainage strategy.

cues.phrase: The drain flushes freely ... little residual free fluid / Replace the existing peritoneal drain
cues.why: The stem explicitly reports that the device functions and there is little undrained fluid, directly removing the replacement option.

cues.phrase: Vasopressor and ventilator support have increased despite ongoing neonatal resuscitation / Continue the current drainage strategy
cues.why: Continued deterioration directly removes unchanged treatment. Laparotomy is the only novel strategy and is selectable through generic failed-treatment escalation.

fairness: Laparotomy for assessment is the best offered plan in the described deteriorating infant with perforated NEC despite drainage. The explanation does not assert that drain output proves adequate source control.

The physiological findings justify escalation, but the two drain choices do not create a substantial resident-level decision against surgery. Naming a patent drain and then choosing the only different treatment is not two consequential clinical inferences.

The later episode supplies perforation, drainage and current decline, so it can stand alone and does not contradict the earlier improving course. Earlier feedback does not state this operative answer.
suggestions: Clarify the response chronology without inventing a universal waiting interval.

items.label: Anatomic review
items.value: The mass is centered in the right kidney; the left kidney is normal. The renal vein and vena cava are patent, and the lesion can be removed intact without resecting an adjacent organ.

items.label: Staging review
items.value: Imaging shows no distant disease. The multidisciplinary radiology review describes the appearance as typical of Wilms tumor; no tissue has yet been obtained.

choices.label: Up-front nephrectomy at the pediatric center
choices.rationale: Under the stated COG pathway, a typical resectable unilateral Wilms-pattern renal mass generally proceeds to nephrectomy. Biopsy first is not required for this presentation and can change local stage.
choices.temptation: Apply resectability and the actual treatment framework together.
choices.correctUnder: Typical resectable unilateral disease in the COG pathway.

choices.label: Core biopsy followed by preoperative chemotherapy
choices.rationale: This is a credible route for atypical or unresectable disease, but the stated anatomy and COG context do not establish that indication.
choices.temptation: Generalize the usual tissue-before-cancer-treatment rule to an exception.
choices.correctUnder: Atypical or inoperable tumor for which primary nephrectomy is not appropriate.

choices.label: Preoperative chemotherapy followed by nephrectomy

choices.temptation: Import the SIOP pathway without applying the explicitly stated framework and anatomy.
choices.correctUnder: A SIOP-aligned protocol or an appropriate COG preoperative-treatment indication.

nodes.explanation: Under the stated COG pathway, a typical resectable unilateral Wilms-pattern renal mass generally proceeds to nephrectomy. Biopsy first is not required for this presentation and can change local stage.

reasoning.interpretation: Assess the unilateral renal origin and intact-resection anatomy as a typical resectable Wilms context.
reasoning.decision: Apply the stated COG framework to choose nephrectomy rather than automatic biopsy or a different protocol sequence.

reasoning.deletionTest: Deleting the framework leaves preoperative chemotherapy defensible; deleting resectability makes biopsy-first competitive. Normal contralateral kidney and vascular/adjacent-organ findings each define a real exception.
reasoning.counterfactual: If the mass required removal of a major adjacent organ to achieve resection, biopsy followed by preoperative chemotherapy would become the best offered pathway.

nodes.objective: Plan regional nodal staging despite normal-appearing nodes.
nodes.currentUpdate: At Noah Bennett's planned outside nephrectomy, the operative team reviews the regional-node plan.
nodes.task: Which regional-node strategy is appropriate during Noah Bennett's nephrectomy?

items.label: Preoperative nodal imaging
items.value: No regional lymph node is enlarged or radiologically suspicious.

items.label: Operative inspection
items.value: The visible regional nodes are small and soft. The kidney mass remains intact without rupture or spill.

choices.label: Sample regional lymph nodes
choices.rationale: Normal size, imaging and gross appearance do not reliably establish negative microscopic nodes. Regional sampling is required for local Wilms staging.
choices.temptation: Distinguish grossly reassuring findings from histologic staging.
choices.correctUnder: Wilms nephrectomy requiring regional staging.

choices.label: Omit regional lymph-node sampling
choices.rationale: Normal imaging and inspection cannot replace histologic regional staging. An intact primary tumor does not establish a negative nodal stage.
choices.temptation: Overread two reassuring but nondefinitive assessments as proof of no nodal disease.
choices.correctUnder: An operation not requiring Wilms tumor regional staging; not this nephrectomy.

choices.label: Perform formal retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy
choices.rationale: The goal is representative regional staging, not routine radical node clearance. Grossly normal nodes do not create an indication for a more extensive dissection.
choices.temptation: Convert the need for some nodal tissue into a therapeutic clearance operation.
choices.correctUnder: A separately established indication for a formal nodal-clearance procedure rather than routine Wilms staging.

nodes.explanation: Normal size, imaging and gross appearance do not reliably establish negative microscopic nodes. Regional sampling is required for local Wilms staging.

reasoning.interpretation: Interpret imaging and inspection as insufficient evidence about microscopic nodal involvement.
reasoning.decision: Choose regional sampling as the appropriate staging scope instead of no sampling or a formal clearance.

reasoning.decidingObservation: Microscopic regional status has not been established despite two normal gross assessments.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Understaging can alter adjuvant treatment selection.
reasoning.deletionTest: Deleting the normal gross findings leaves the rule but removes the plausible reason a resident would omit sampling; they are needed to test the evidence-limit error. Intact primary status distinguishes an independent spill issue.
reasoning.counterfactual: If the current operation were for a non-Wilms benign renal process with no oncologic staging indication, omission of regional sampling would become reasonable.

items.label: Anatomical report
items.value: The left suprarenal mass displaces the kidney inferiorly and surrounds the origins of the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries. There is no renal-parenchymal mass or distant disease on staging studies.

items.label: Biochemical record
items.value: Urinary VMA and HVA are above the laboratory's age-adjusted reference ranges. No tissue diagnosis is available.

choices.label: Obtain a core biopsy for tumor characterization
choices.rationale: The extrarenal catecholamine-associated pattern suggests a neuroblastic tumor, and major-vessel encasement is an imaging-defined surgical risk. Obtain tissue to guide risk-based therapy rather than attempt an up-front definitive resection.
choices.temptation: Distinguish a neuroblastic surgical-risk pattern from a typical resectable renal mass.
choices.correctUnder: A neuroblastic mass with imaging-defined risk factors.

choices.label: Attempt complete up-front tumor resection

choices.temptation: Equate localized disease with surgically low-risk disease.
choices.correctUnder: A suitable localized tumor without imaging-defined surgical risk factors after specialist review.

choices.temptation: Apply the no-biopsy Wilms exception to every childhood abdominal mass.
choices.correctUnder: A typical resectable unilateral renal tumor in a COG-aligned pathway.

nodes.objective: Balance prematurity-related respiratory risk against reducible hernia risk.
nodes.currentUpdate: Henry Parker was born at 26 weeks and remains in an outside neonatal unit. Discharge is being planned with ongoing respiratory follow-up.
nodes.task: Which repair-timing plan is most appropriate for Henry Parker's current groin finding?

items.label: Groin course
items.value: Pediatric surgical examinations repeatedly show an inguinal bulge that reduces completely. There have been no painful irreducible episodes, vomiting or skin changes.

items.label: Respiratory and follow-up context
items.value: He still needs oxygen for bronchopulmonary dysplasia. His family can attend surgical follow-up and has been taught the warning signs requiring urgent reassessment.

choices.label: Plan repair after the neonatal hospitalization
choices.rationale: For a currently reducible hernia in a very preterm infant with ongoing respiratory disease, a delayed planned repair with follow-up is reasonable. The timing balances respiratory risk against incarceration during the wait; it is not indefinite observation or a universal age rule.
choices.temptation: Apply the respiratory-risk and hernia-urgency findings together.
choices.correctUnder: Selected reducible hernia with substantial prematurity-related respiratory risk and a reliable follow-up plan.

choices.label: Plan repair before neonatal discharge
choices.rationale: Earlier repair limits the time exposed to incarceration risk, but carries respiratory tradeoffs in this infant. No current incarceration complication requires overriding the respiratory consideration in the offered comparison.
choices.temptation: Treat every pediatric hernia as requiring repair before the current hospitalization ends.
choices.correctUnder: A changed hernia course or patient/follow-up factors making delay less appropriate after specialist review.

choices.label: Use serial surveillance for spontaneous resolution
choices.rationale: The current record repeatedly demonstrates a hernia, rather than documented resolution. Its reducibility supports a planned timing discussion, not a presumption that repair will become unnecessary. Reassessment remains part of the delayed surgical plan.
choices.temptation: Treat the possibility of spontaneous resolution as sufficient reason to abandon a planned repair pathway.
choices.correctUnder: A subsequently resolved finding confirmed on surgical reassessment with a revised diagnosis/plan, not the repeatedly demonstrated current hernia.

nodes.explanation: For a currently reducible hernia in a very preterm infant with ongoing respiratory disease, a delayed planned repair with follow-up is reasonable. The timing balances respiratory risk against incarceration during the wait; it is not indefinite observation or a universal age rule.

reasoning.interpretation: Recognize a reducible hernia without current incarceration while interpreting ongoing prematurity-related respiratory disease.
reasoning.decision: Balance the competing hazards and choose a scheduled delayed strategy instead of a compulsory pre-discharge repair or indefinite surveillance.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Require before-discharge repair solely because this is a child, despite current respiratory comorbidity.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The hernia remains reducible without acute episodes while respiratory disease persists and follow-up is workable.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Unnecessary respiratory morbidity or, at the opposite extreme, an unmonitored delay could follow.
reasoning.deletionTest: Deleting respiratory disease removes the reason to favor delay; deleting the reducibility/episode history removes the safety boundary. Follow-up context is necessary to the real tradeoff rather than a permission that surgery is available.
reasoning.counterfactual: If painful irreducible episodes emerged or reliable follow-up could not be maintained, an earlier repair plan could become preferable after urgent specialist reassessment.

authorGate.coverTheKeyCueAttack: No exact repair age, trial threshold, oxygen dose or effect size is supplied. The two planned timing options are genuine competitors. The surveillance label names a positive strategy rather than advertising an incomplete plan; the persistent examination finding must be applied.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Timing of an already indicated pediatric repair; no technique or anesthesia comparison is smuggled in.
authorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Recognize a reducible hernia without current incarceration while interpreting ongoing prematurity-related respiratory disease. Then Balance the competing hazards and choose a scheduled delayed strategy instead of a compulsory pre-discharge repair or indefinite surveillance.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: competing real harms distinguish this from the former obvious referral question. The clinical ranking is conditional and must be reviewed by Melissa.
authorGate.oneBestAnswer: The hernia remains reducible without acute episodes while respiratory disease persists and follow-up is workable. Counterfactual: If painful irreducible episodes emerged or reliable follow-up could not be maintained, an earlier repair plan could become preferable after urgent specialist reassessment.
authorGate.sequenceAndFiniteProfileAttack: Single node. No parent video or previous fluid-only scan supplies tissue identity; the actual pediatric surgical examinations establish the finding.
authorGate.repairAndRecheck: Replaced the superficial referral/urgency contrast with a respiratory-versus-incarceration tradeoff and removed the trial-specific age cutoff; re-solved all timing plans. Final option recheck removed the phrase without a repair plan from the surveillance label, kept the same documented-persistence discriminator and re-solved the three strategies. Exact clinical ranking still needs named review.
authorGate.remainingRisk: The 2025 syntheses differ on incarceration estimates. No disputed claim of zero incarceration risk is taught. Delayed timing is a reasonable patient-specific proposal, not universally mandatory.
authorGate.verdict: Draft for independent review; author self-check is not PASS

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should follow {patientName}'s current records?

answerChoices.label: Complete an upper-GI contrast examination
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent green drainage still requires assessment of intestinal rotation. The actual acquisition did not image the required duodenal course, so gastric emptying does not resolve that question.

answerChoices.label: Obtain a targeted pyloric ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: A pyloric study addresses gastric-outlet obstruction; it does not replace the incomplete assessment prompted by persistent green drainage.

answerChoices.label: Obtain a water-soluble contrast enema
answerChoices.rationale: The record raises an unresolved proximal rotational problem rather than an established distal meconium obstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Persistent green drainage still requires assessment of intestinal rotation. The actual acquisition did not image the required duodenal course, so gastric emptying does not resolve that question.

items.label: Abdominal examination and film
items.value: The abdomen is soft. Plain radiography shows gas through the bowel without a fixed obstructive pattern.

items.label: Contrast acquisition record
items.value: The completed acquisition stops after contrast leaves the duodenal bulb; the remainder of the duodenal course was not imaged. The report describes gastric emptying.

items.label: Clinical course
items.value: Green gastric drainage continues; temperature and the inflammatory evaluation have not suggested infection.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Subsequent outside record for {patientName}: the contrast study has been completed, and the hospital team is reassessing the new observations below.
decisionNodes.stem: Which plan should the outside surgical team select for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Proceed to urgent operative exploration
answerChoices.rationale: The completed study plus worsening abdominal and perfusion findings supports urgent exploration for volvulus, with bowel viability assessed during surgery. Further diagnostic observation risks ongoing ischemia.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the upper-GI contrast examination
answerChoices.rationale: The rotational examination is now complete and has identified volvulus. Repeating it does not address deteriorating perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Continue gastric decompression and reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Decompression and fluids remain background care, but they do not correct the documented volvulus while perfusion worsens.

decisionNodes.explanation: The completed study plus worsening abdominal and perfusion findings supports urgent exploration for volvulus, with bowel viability assessed during surgery. Further diagnostic observation risks ongoing ischemia.

items.label: Change during resuscitation
items.value: The abdomen becomes tender and mottled. Perfusion and urine output worsen, and lactate rises despite IV fluid treatment.
